Get trending papers in your email inbox! # Daily Papers ## by[AK](/akhaliq) and the research community ![](/front/assets/papers-by.png) ### [StepAudio 3 Realtime Technical Report](/papers/2609.14005) Realtime spoken interaction demands deep reasoning, prompt responses, and fluid turn-taking. We present StepAudio 3 Realtime, an audio-language foundation model organized around a continuous listen-converse-think-act loop. Deep Perception captures rich acoustic cues to interpret user intent, while Seamless Duplex models synchronized audio streams to handle pauses, backchannels, and interruptions naturally. Crucially, we resolve the tension between deep deliberation and latency via Think-While-Speaking, executing private reasoning in parallel with spoken delivery. In reasoning mode, StepAudio 3 reaches a 73.0 macro average on StepAudioChat. With Think-While-Speaking, it achieves dialogue and reasoning performance comparable to dedicated reasoning models while speaking in real time. Furthermore, an integrated Voice Agent handles asynchronous tool execution without disrupting the dialogue flow. StepAudio 3 Realtime achieves top-tier performance across key dimensions: an exceptional 90.6 on the MMSU benchmark, 98.9 Overall on the Artificial Analysis Full-Duplex Bench, and a 56.0% macro task-success rate on τ-Voice. ![stepfun-ai](https://cdn-avatars.huggingface.co/v1/production/uploads/644f7e6233ac8f46fa0b9e26/CmF2ocXhkr2UtHXgmwq7-.png) ### [OmniFlatten: An End-to-end GPT Model for Seamless Voice Conversation](/papers/2410.17799) Full-duplex spoken dialogue systems significantly advance over traditional turn-based dialogue systems, as they allow simultaneous bidirectional communication, closely mirroring human-human interactions. However, achieving low latency and natural interactions in full-duplex dialogue systems remains a significant challenge, especially considering human conversation dynamics such as interruptions, backchannels, and overlapping speech. In this paper, we introduce a novel End-to-End GPT-based model OmniFlatten for full-duplex conversation, capable of effectively modeling the complex behaviors inherent to natural conversations with low latency. To achieve full-duplex communication capabilities, we propose a multi-stage post-training scheme that progressively adapts a text-based large language model (LLM) backbone into a speech-text dialogue LLM, capable of generating text and speech in real time, without modifying the architecture of the backbone LLM. The training process comprises three stages: modality alignment, half-duplex dialogue learning, and full-duplex dialogue learning. Throughout all training stages, we standardize the data using a flattening operation, which allows us to unify the training methods and the model architecture across different modalities and tasks. Our approach offers a straightforward modeling technique and a promising research direction for developing efficient and natural end-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue systems. Audio samples of dialogues generated by OmniFlatten can be found at this web site (https://omniflatten.github.io/). ![](/avatars/cd88dc48e8200d4c32f7b233dc72a16e.svg) ### [Overcoming State Inertia in Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models via Activation Steering](/papers/2606.11386) Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) enable seamless speech interaction by allowing models to listen and speak simultaneously, yet the internal mechanism by which they coordinate listening and speaking remains underexplored. Describe the issue below: ![](/static/base/1.0.1/images/icons/smileybones-small.svg) ![arXiv logo](/static/base/1.0.1/images/arxiv-logo-primary-light.svg) # LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences ###### Abstract Traditional evaluation benchmarks reduce inherently interconnected scientific knowledge in life sciences into flat lists of questions, disregarding the underlying topological structure of the knowledge. We introduce, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences, featuring over 10,000 high-quality multiple-choice questions across medicine, biology, and chemistry. Our approach constructs a weighted evaluation graph using bidirectional matching and semantic similarity algorithms, where nodes represent questions and edge weights capture their semantic relationships. Leveraging this graph topology, we design two novel evaluation metrics. The Global Coherence Score (GCS) measures a model’s consistency within semantically related neighborhoods, while Knowledge Balance Score (KBS) analyzes how model errors are distributed across the graph to reveal conceptual blind spots. LG-Bench facilitates fine-grained comparison of LLMs by surfacing differences in conceptual coherence and patterns of knowledge organization across models. Our framework shifts the evaluation paradigm from flat accuracy metrics to structure-aware analysis, offering a new lens for diagnosing and improving LLM performance in the life sciences domain. ## 1 Introduction ![Refer to caption](2610.26787v1/pic/546fc80798856dcf683f5dc6e3170b3c.jpg) Recent breakthroughs in large language models (LLMs) epitomized by systems have rapidly accelerated progress in natural language processing and sparked an intense wave of research activity across multiple scientific disciplines. As model scale and performance continue to increase, the community is increasingly dependent on systematic evaluation to guide development, compare approaches, and guarantee safe deployment. ![Refer to caption](2610.26787v1/benchmark-overview.png) However, current evaluations such as practices in artificial intelligence suffer from a fundamental misrepresentation: they treat knowledge as isolated, independent facts when it naturally forms interconnected webs of understanding. This "flat-world illusion" is particularly problematic in complex domains such as life sciences ([Bodenreider, 2004](#bib.bib1); [Jin et al., 2021](#bib.bib2)), where understanding protein function requires grasping its role in cellular pathways, regulatory mechanisms, and therapeutic implications as an integrated whole. Traditional benchmarks present evaluation questions as flat lists, obscuring the rich semantic relationships that define genuine domain expertise. These limitations make it hard for current metrics to distinguish between genuine understanding and mere pattern matching. To address this gap, we introduce LG-Bench, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences evaluation. As shown in Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences"), LG-Bench contains over 10k expert-reviewed questions drawn from recent peer-reviewed literature across Medicine, Biology, and Chemistry, with representative sources including Nature, Science, and Cell. The benchmark is designed to cover both foundational knowledge and recent scientific findings, making it suitable for evaluating whether models can organize concepts rather than only recall isolated facts. Using bidirectional matching and semantic similarity, we transform the question corpus into a weighted evaluation graph whose edges capture relationships between semantically related questions. This graph makes local neighborhoods of related scientific concepts explicit, enabling evaluation beyond flat accuracy by measuring knowledge coherence and the topological distribution of model errors. highlights.content: ![]() ![PR Newswire](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/pr_newswire--theme-light.svg) ![PR Newswire](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/pr_newswire--theme-dark.svg) # llm-d 1.0 Advances Open, Cost-Efficient AI Inference for Production Scale ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/international-bus-mach.svg) SAN JOSE, Calif., Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, llm-d project contributors announced the release of llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for the open source project designed to help organizations deploy and scale large language model inference more efficiently across modern infrastructure. Founded in 2025 by Red Hat, IBM (NYSE: IBM), Google Cloud, CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), llm-d plays a key role in the open foundation for enterprises deploying AI at scale in production. As organizations race to put AI into production, many are discovering that running AI at scale can be as challenging and expensive as building the models themselves. Organizations need a way to deliver responsive experiences for users, support agentic workloads, and maximize utilization of increasingly scarce compute resources. llm-d 1.0 is built to address these challenges through intelligent distributed inference capabilities to facilitate improvements in performance, increases in throughput and help organizations gain greater control over the economics of AI serving. **Turning Innovation into Production Reality** With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Agentic workloads continually access and reuse vast amounts of context while supporting parallel agents that can generate unpredictable bursts of activity. Managing that context often consumes more resources than generating the final output itself, making latency, throughput, memory efficiency and infrastructure costs critical factors in realizing AI ROI. llm-d already delivers hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box for complex infrastructure environments, as well as prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch and async inference — across multiple model servers, including vLLM and SGLang. llm-d 1.0 is engineered to bring that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations and the ongoing work of running inference in production: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, providing with zero downtime features and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into a platform. New capabilities in 1.0 include: The result is infrastructure that can support diverse AI workloads, ranging from latency-sensitive user interactions to large-scale autonomous agent workflows, without forcing organizations to choose between responsiveness and efficiency. **Growing Ecosystem Momentum** llm-d is already being used across a growing ecosystem of model developers, cloud providers, infrastructure vendors and enterprise users. Today, the project includes more than 500 contributors from over 25 organizations collaborating on the future of distributed AI serving and helping build common foundations across the AI infrastructure stack. Core users including organizations running large-scale distributed inference, frontier model developers optimizing inference stacks and cloud providers serving multi-tenant AI endpoints have all seen measurable benefit from deploying llm-d. highlights.content: [IBM Newsroom](index.php) # All press releases # llm-d 1.0 Advances Open, Cost-Efficient AI Inference for Production Scale • llm-d 1.0 consolidates a hardened core for distributed inference validated for day 2 production deployments that helps organizations improve AI serving efficiency and scale enterprise workloads. • llm-d is broadly adopted and trusted by frontier model labs, hyperscalers and neoclouds, hardware accelerators, and major enterprises, with recent demonstrations showing up to five to 10 times cost reductions for context-heavy agentic workloads [1] and three times greater output throughput. [2] Oct 20, 2026 ![](/image/iso_banner.png) **SAN JOSE, C.A., OCT. 20, 2026** – Today, llm-d project contributors announced the release of llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for the open source project designed to help organizations deploy and scale large language model inference more efficiently across modern infrastructure. Founded [in 2025](https://llm-d.ai/blog/llm-d-press-release) by Red Hat, IBM (NYSE: [IBM](http://www.ibm.com/investor)), Google Cloud, CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), llm-d plays a key role in the open foundation for enterprises deploying AI at scale in production. As organizations race to put AI into production, many are discovering that running AI at scale can be as challenging and expensive as building the models themselves. Organizations need a way to deliver responsive experiences for users, support agentic workloads, and maximize utilization of increasingly scarce compute resources. llm-d 1.0 is built to address these challenges through intelligent distributed inference capabilities to facilitate improvements in performance, increases in throughput and help organizations gain greater control over the economics of AI serving. **Turning Innovation into Production Reality** With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Agentic workloads continually access and reuse vast amounts of context while supporting parallel agents that can generate unpredictable bursts of activity. Managing that context often consumes more resources than generating the final output itself, making latency, throughput, memory efficiency and infrastructure costs critical factors in realizing AI ROI. llm-d already delivers hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box for complex infrastructure environments, as well as prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch and async inference — across multiple model servers, including vLLM and SGLang. llm-d 1.0 is engineered to bring that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations and the ongoing work of running inference in production: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, providing with zero downtime features and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into a platform. New capabilities in 1.0 include: * **Multi-tenant quality of service** — Priority and fairness-aware flow control helps latency-sensitive requests, and bursty agent workloads share a fleet without starving one another. * **Zero-downtime operations** — Router high availability with hot standby and rolling updates keep traffic flowing through upgrades and planned maintenance. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # VS Code 1.137 Puts AI Agents in Dev Containers [2026] ![Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/hvogel.webp) [Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/author/hvogel/) Updated Oct 20, 2026 · 15 min read Microsoft has quietly turned its most popular code editor into something closer to an operating system for AI agents. Visual Studio Code 1.137, released September 9, 2026, and the follow-up update that landed roughly a week later, add a feature Microsoft calls the Agent Host system: an architecture that lets multiple AI coding agents run as managed processes inside the editor, each with its own isolated Dev Container, its own tools, and its own dependencies. Paired with new automations and a voice mode, the release marks the clearest sign yet that Microsoft sees the editor’s future as a control center for autonomous software work, not just a faster autocomplete box. The timing matters. The update landed in the same month Google opened Gemini 4 Argon to public developer access, OpenAI pushed GPT-6 Astra’s programming-language coverage past 87%, and DeepSeek shipped a coding-focused model built for end-to-end project work. VS Code’s agent infrastructure isn’t arriving in a vacuum. It’s arriving right as the underlying models get cheap and capable enough to actually run unattended for long stretches, which is the whole point of giving them a container to live in. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What the Agent Host System Actually Does According to the [official VS Code 1.137 release notes](https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_137), the update reworks how the editor manages AI-driven processes. Instead of treating an AI coding assistant as a single chat panel bolted onto the sidebar, the Agent Host system gives each agent session its own managed runtime. That runtime can be spun up, paused, monitored, and torn down independently of the editor’s main process, which is the kind of plumbing you’d expect from a container orchestrator, not a text editor. Developer coverage of the release, including a [write-up on DEV Community](https://dev.to/hamidrazadev/vs-code-1137-is-here-automations-voice-mode-and-the-features-thatll-change-how-you-code-lgg), frames 1.137 as pushing the editor “closer to a real AI-powered coding partner” rather than a passive tool. The practical upshot: a developer can now kick off a background agent to refactor a module, keep working in the foreground on something else, and check back on the agent’s progress without losing their own editor state. ## Agents Now Run Inside Dev Containers The headline technical change is that agents can run inside local Dev Containers, each preloaded with the project’s own tools and dependencies. That’s a meaningful shift from running an agent directly against a developer’s host machine. A Dev Container gives the agent a sandboxed, reproducible environment that matches the project’s actual build and test setup, rather than whatever happens to be installed globally on the developer’s laptop. Industry analysis published around the update, including a piece from [Analytics Insight](https://www.analyticsinsight.net/artificial-intelligence/how-ai-is-changing-code-editors-in-2026), describes this as part of a broader pattern: “code editors become agent workspaces” where “one editor can handle many agents” at once. That framing lines up with what Microsoft shipped. The container boundary isn’t just a convenience, it’s a safety mechanism. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Intel’s 480GB AI Chip Takes Aim at Nvidia, AMD [2026] ![Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/droth.webp) [Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/author/droth/) Updated Oct 20, 2026 · 14 min read Intel used the Open Compute Project Global Summit this month to put a name and a full spec sheet on the AI chip it had been teasing for more than a year. The Intel GPU D-series, built on the Xe3P architecture and previously known under the codename Crescent Island, packs up to 480GB of LPDDR5X memory onto a single air-cooled PCIe card. TechRadar framed the announcement under the headline “Inference is becoming the defining AI workload,” and that framing gets at what makes this launch worth paying attention to on October 20, 2026: Intel is not trying to out-FLOP Nvidia or AMD. It is trying to out-fit them, cramming more model into a single card so data centers need fewer cards to serve the same request. That distinction matters because the AI inference GPU market has quietly become the most contested piece of real estate in the data center. Training clusters get the headlines and the eye-watering price tags, but inference, the actual serving of chatbot replies, coding suggestions and agentic tasks to paying users, is where the volume lives and where the margins get squeezed. Intel’s bet is that memory capacity per card, not raw petaflops, is the lever that actually moves serving costs. Whether that bet pays off depends on factors Intel has not yet disclosed: price, availability, and independent benchmarks. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Intel Actually Announced at OCP 2026 The headline numbers, confirmed across multiple outlets covering the Open Compute Project Global Summit, are specific. The Intel GPU D-series delivers up to 480GB of LPDDR5X memory, 1.5TB/s of memory bandwidth, and 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute, all inside a 350-watt envelope that fits a standard, air-cooled PCIe card. That last detail is not a footnote. Most high-memory AI accelerators demand liquid cooling and custom rack infrastructure; Intel is explicitly positioning the D-series to drop into server chassis that already exist, according to coverage from [StorageReview](https://www.storagereview.com/news/intel-gpu-d-series-480gb-lpddr5x-1-3-pflops-fp8-350w-pcie-card). There is a wrinkle in the headline figure worth flagging before anyone builds a budget around it. The 480GB ceiling applies only to partner-built cards from ODMs and server vendors. Intel’s own branded card carries 160GB, a meaningful gap that [XenoSpectrum’s breakdown of the D-series memory tiers](https://xenospectrum.com/en/intel-d-series-inference-memory-bandwidth/) lays out in detail. Intel’s product page for the [GPU D270, its inference-optimized data center card](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/products/details/discrete-gpus/data-center-gpu/d-series.html), confirms the 480GB LPDDR5X figure as the top-end configuration rather than a universal spec across every SKU. Intel says a single D-series card can host models of up to roughly 300 billion parameters, and that an eight-GPU system can support more than one trillion parameters in aggregate. Those are Intel’s own claims, disclosed at the summit rather than validated by a third-party benchmark. AI Agents.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # VS Code 1.137 Puts AI Agents in Dev Containers [2026] ![Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/hvogel.webp) [Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/author/hvogel/) Updated Oct 20, 2026 · 15 min read Microsoft has quietly turned its most popular code editor into something closer to an operating system for AI agents. Visual Studio Code 1.137, released September 9, 2026, and the follow-up update that landed roughly a week later, add a feature Microsoft calls the Agent Host system: an architecture that lets multiple AI coding agents run as managed processes inside the editor, each with its own isolated Dev Container, its own tools, and its own dependencies. Paired with new automations and a voice mode, the release marks the clearest sign yet that Microsoft sees the editor’s future as a control center for autonomous software work, not just a faster autocomplete box. The timing matters. The update landed in the same month Google opened Gemini 4 Argon to public developer access, OpenAI pushed GPT-6 Astra’s programming-language coverage past 87%, and DeepSeek shipped a coding-focused model built for end-to-end project work. VS Code’s agent infrastructure isn’t arriving in a vacuum. It’s arriving right as the underlying models get cheap and capable enough to actually run unattended for long stretches, which is the whole point of giving them a container to live in. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What the Agent Host System Actually Does According to the [official VS Code 1.137 release notes](https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_137), the update reworks how the editor manages AI-driven processes. Instead of treating an AI coding assistant as a single chat panel bolted onto the sidebar, the Agent Host system gives each agent session its own managed runtime. That runtime can be spun up, paused, monitored, and torn down independently of the editor’s main process, which is the kind of plumbing you’d expect from a container orchestrator, not a text editor. Developer coverage of the release, including a [write-up on DEV Community](https://dev.to/hamidrazadev/vs-code-1137-is-here-automations-voice-mode-and-the-features-thatll-change-how-you-code-lgg), frames 1.137 as pushing the editor “closer to a real AI-powered coding partner” rather than a passive tool. The practical upshot: a developer can now kick off a background agent to refactor a module, keep working in the foreground on something else, and check back on the agent’s progress without losing their own editor state. ## Agents Now Run Inside Dev Containers The headline technical change is that agents can run inside local Dev Containers, each preloaded with the project’s own tools and dependencies. That’s a meaningful shift from running an agent directly against a developer’s host machine. A Dev Container gives the agent a sandboxed, reproducible environment that matches the project’s actual build and test setup, rather than whatever happens to be installed globally on the developer’s laptop. Industry analysis published around the update, including a piece from [Analytics Insight](https://www.analyticsinsight.net/artificial-intelligence/how-ai-is-changing-code-editors-in-2026), describes this as part of a broader pattern: “code editors become agent workspaces” where “one editor can handle many agents” at once. That framing lines up with what Microsoft shipped. The container boundary isn’t just a convenience, it’s a safety mechanism. AI Agents.content: ![](https://www.techtarget.com/rms/onlineimages/security_g1185245180_searchsitetablet_520X173.jpg) Getty Images/iStockphoto # AI agents risk blind spots without shared security data, experts warn ## Building a common, continuously updated view across security tools raises practical questions about data ownership, freshness and resolving disagreements. ![Nathan Eddy](https://cdn.ttgtmedia.com/rms/onlineimages/nathan_eddy.jpg) A security tool reports that a server is patched, while another identifies it as vulnerable. This can leave analysts investigating which record is correct. However, an AI agent relying solely on one of those findings could recommend a response before that conflict is resolved. When security tools contradict each other, is letting AI break the tie efficient automation -- or a disaster waiting to happen? With organizations rapidly introducing agents into security operations, analysts and automated systems need access to the same asset identities, exposure information and business context. But combining records does not establish their accuracy. A shared view must preserve evidence, expose unresolved disagreements and carry corrections into decisions already underway. Michelle Abraham, research vice president for security and trust at research firm IDC, said organizations should prioritize information that explains an asset's reachability, business importance, controls and current condition over vulnerability severity alone. "An AI agent's recommendation is only as trustworthy as the asset inventory and control taxonomy feeding it," she explained. ## Build a common foundation for decisions Agents should seek additional information when the available evidence is insufficient, Abraham added, just as an analyst would. If further investigation remains inconclusive, the issue should be escalated to a human reviewer. The [shared data layer](https://www.techtarget.com/data-technologies/opinion/Why-AI-should-build-on-not-copy-your-data-stack) should consistently identify each asset and link it to business and technical owners, services, exposure, compensating controls and exceptions. Freshness should be tracked explicitly, while raw data can remain in the underlying tools. Security should own the system that reconciles those records, Abraham said, but responsibility for individual facts remains distributed. Business owners understand service criticality and accepted risks; technical owners maintain information about software, reachability and vulnerabilities. "When updates are required, the data layer has to be corrected, not the dashboard layer," she said. She recommended bidirectional connections among asset management, security monitoring and exposure management systems so corrections do not require separate manual updates. Otherwise, a dashboard can display an amended record while another tool continues supplying an agent with the earlier version. ## Preserve conflicts and recheck changing conditions Some apparent disagreements reflect different aspects of the same risk, said Diana Kelley, CISO at AI security and governance specialist Noma Security. A vulnerable system can also be effectively isolated from the network. Both findings may be accurate, and the assessment needs to account for them together. A contradictory patch status requires investigation into the asset identity, software version, evidence source and observation time. "A newer timestamp alone does not make a finding correct," she said. The shared view should retain unresolved conflicts and provide access to the underlying evidence. Analysts and agents need to understand why a recommendation was made, rather than receive a risk score stripped of its supporting facts. Freshness requirements should also reflect how quickly a condition changes and the consequences of acting on it. An asset's owner may remain unchanged for months; network exposure can change within a minute. "Check when the condition was observed, not just when the dashboard updated," ...

Get trending papers in your email inbox! # Daily Papers ## by[AK](/akhaliq) and the research community ![](/front/assets/papers-by.png) ### [StepAudio 3 Realtime Technical Report](/papers/2609.14005) Realtime spoken interaction demands deep reasoning, prompt responses, and fluid turn-taking. We present StepAudio 3 Realtime, an audio-language foundation model organized around a continuous listen-converse-think-act loop. Deep Perception captures rich acoustic cues to interpret user intent, while Seamless Duplex models synchronized audio streams to handle pauses, backchannels, and interruptions naturally. Crucially, we resolve the tension between deep deliberation and latency via Think-While-Speaking, executing private reasoning in parallel with spoken delivery. In reasoning mode, StepAudio 3 reaches a 73.0 macro average on StepAudioChat. With Think-While-Speaking, it achieves dialogue and reasoning performance comparable to dedicated reasoning models while speaking in real time. Furthermore, an integrated Voice Agent handles asynchronous tool execution without disrupting the dialogue flow. StepAudio 3 Realtime achieves top-tier performance across key dimensions: an exceptional 90.6 on the MMSU benchmark, 98.9 Overall on the Artificial Analysis Full-Duplex Bench, and a 56.0% macro task-success rate on τ-Voice. ![stepfun-ai](https://cdn-avatars.huggingface.co/v1/production/uploads/644f7e6233ac8f46fa0b9e26/CmF2ocXhkr2UtHXgmwq7-.png) ### [OmniFlatten: An End-to-end GPT Model for Seamless Voice Conversation](/papers/2410.17799) Full-duplex spoken dialogue systems significantly advance over traditional turn-based dialogue systems, as they allow simultaneous bidirectional communication, closely mirroring human-human interactions. However, achieving low latency and natural interactions in full-duplex dialogue systems remains a significant challenge, especially considering human conversation dynamics such as interruptions, backchannels, and overlapping speech. In this paper, we introduce a novel End-to-End GPT-based model OmniFlatten for full-duplex conversation, capable of effectively modeling the complex behaviors inherent to natural conversations with low latency. To achieve full-duplex communication capabilities, we propose a multi-stage post-training scheme that progressively adapts a text-based large language model (LLM) backbone into a speech-text dialogue LLM, capable of generating text and speech in real time, without modifying the architecture of the backbone LLM. The training process comprises three stages: modality alignment, half-duplex dialogue learning, and full-duplex dialogue learning. Throughout all training stages, we standardize the data using a flattening operation, which allows us to unify the training methods and the model architecture across different modalities and tasks. Our approach offers a straightforward modeling technique and a promising research direction for developing efficient and natural end-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue systems. Audio samples of dialogues generated by OmniFlatten can be found at this web site (https://omniflatten.github.io/). ![](/avatars/cd88dc48e8200d4c32f7b233dc72a16e.svg) ### [Overcoming State Inertia in Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models via Activation Steering](/papers/2606.11386) Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) enable seamless speech interaction by allowing models to listen and speak simultaneously, yet the internal mechanism by which they coordinate listening and speaking remains underexplored. Describe the issue below: ![](/static/base/1.0.1/images/icons/smileybones-small.svg) ![arXiv logo](/static/base/1.0.1/images/arxiv-logo-primary-light.svg) # LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences ###### Abstract Traditional evaluation benchmarks reduce inherently interconnected scientific knowledge in life sciences into flat lists of questions, disregarding the underlying topological structure of the knowledge. We introduce, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences, featuring over 10,000 high-quality multiple-choice questions across medicine, biology, and chemistry. Our approach constructs a weighted evaluation graph using bidirectional matching and semantic similarity algorithms, where nodes represent questions and edge weights capture their semantic relationships. Leveraging this graph topology, we design two novel evaluation metrics. The Global Coherence Score (GCS) measures a model’s consistency within semantically related neighborhoods, while Knowledge Balance Score (KBS) analyzes how model errors are distributed across the graph to reveal conceptual blind spots. LG-Bench facilitates fine-grained comparison of LLMs by surfacing differences in conceptual coherence and patterns of knowledge organization across models. Our framework shifts the evaluation paradigm from flat accuracy metrics to structure-aware analysis, offering a new lens for diagnosing and improving LLM performance in the life sciences domain. ## 1 Introduction ![Refer to caption](2610.26787v1/pic/546fc80798856dcf683f5dc6e3170b3c.jpg) Recent breakthroughs in large language models (LLMs) epitomized by systems have rapidly accelerated progress in natural language processing and sparked an intense wave of research activity across multiple scientific disciplines. As model scale and performance continue to increase, the community is increasingly dependent on systematic evaluation to guide development, compare approaches, and guarantee safe deployment. ![Refer to caption](2610.26787v1/benchmark-overview.png) However, current evaluations such as practices in artificial intelligence suffer from a fundamental misrepresentation: they treat knowledge as isolated, independent facts when it naturally forms interconnected webs of understanding. This "flat-world illusion" is particularly problematic in complex domains such as life sciences ([Bodenreider, 2004](#bib.bib1); [Jin et al., 2021](#bib.bib2)), where understanding protein function requires grasping its role in cellular pathways, regulatory mechanisms, and therapeutic implications as an integrated whole. Traditional benchmarks present evaluation questions as flat lists, obscuring the rich semantic relationships that define genuine domain expertise. These limitations make it hard for current metrics to distinguish between genuine understanding and mere pattern matching. To address this gap, we introduce LG-Bench, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences evaluation. As shown in Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences"), LG-Bench contains over 10k expert-reviewed questions drawn from recent peer-reviewed literature across Medicine, Biology, and Chemistry, with representative sources including Nature, Science, and Cell. The benchmark is designed to cover both foundational knowledge and recent scientific findings, making it suitable for evaluating whether models can organize concepts rather than only recall isolated facts. Using bidirectional matching and semantic similarity, we transform the question corpus into a weighted evaluation graph whose edges capture relationships between semantically related questions. This graph makes local neighborhoods of related scientific concepts explicit, enabling evaluation beyond flat accuracy by measuring knowledge coherence and the topological distribution of model errors. As organizations race to put AI into production, many are discovering that running AI at scale can be as challenging and expensive as building the models themselves. Organizations need a way to deliver responsive experiences for users, support agentic workloads, and maximize utilization of increasingly scarce compute resources. llm-d 1.0 is built to address these challenges through intelligent distributed inference capabilities to facilitate improvements in performance, increases in throughput and help organizations gain greater control over the economics of AI serving. **Turning Innovation into Production Reality** With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Agentic workloads continually access and reuse vast amounts of context while supporting parallel agents that can generate unpredictable bursts of activity. Managing that context often consumes more resources than generating the final output itself, making latency, throughput, memory efficiency and infrastructure costs critical factors in realizing AI ROI. llm-d already delivers hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box for complex infrastructure environments, as well as prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch and async inference — across multiple model servers, including vLLM and SGLang. llm-d 1.0 is engineered to bring that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations and the ongoing work of running inference in production: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, providing with zero downtime features and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into a platform. New capabilities in 1.0 include: The result is infrastructure that can support diverse AI workloads, ranging from latency-sensitive user interactions to large-scale autonomous agent workflows, without forcing organizations to choose between responsiveness and efficiency. **Growing Ecosystem Momentum** llm-d is already being used across a growing ecosystem of model developers, cloud providers, infrastructure vendors and enterprise users. Today, the project includes more than 500 contributors from over 25 organizations collaborating on the future of distributed AI serving and helping build common foundations across the AI infrastructure stack. LLMs.titleZh: DeepSeek Opens DeepInfer, Presses OpenAI, Anthropic
LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # DeepSeek Opens DeepInfer, Presses OpenAI, Anthropic [2026] ![Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/mbell.webp) [Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/author/mbell/) Updated Oct 21, 2026 · 15 min read DeepSeek has pulled back the curtain on the software that runs its own AI servers. On October 20, 2026, the Chinese AI company released **DeepInfer**, described as its in-house inference framework, as free and open-source code under the Apache 2.0 license. The move, first flagged widely after [Gizmodo reported it as DeepSeek “dialing up the pressure” on OpenAI and Anthropic](https://gizmodo.com/deepseek-dials-up-the-pressure-on-openai-and-anthropic-with-open-source-inference-tool-2000828261), hands outside developers a working copy of the engine DeepSeek uses to serve its own models at scale, rather than just another research paper or weights dump. The release is narrow by design. DeepInfer currently supports only one model, **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash**, and it ships as offline inference software rather than a finished managed cloud product. But the symbolism is hard to miss: a company based in Hangzhou, formally named **Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co. Ltd.**, is now giving away the exact kind of production-serving code that OpenAI and Anthropic have kept locked inside their own data centers. For a US and global audience watching the AI infrastructure race, that is the story worth unpacking. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What DeepSeek Actually Released on October 20 DeepInfer is DeepSeek’s name for what the company calls its “in-house inference framework.” According to the official GitHub repository and companion documentation, the code was published on October 20, 2026, and immediately made available for anyone to download, inspect, and modify under the Apache 2.0 license. That license matters: it is one of the most permissive open-source terms available, allowing commercial use, modification, and redistribution without requiring the resulting product to be open-sourced in turn. Alongside DeepInfer, DeepSeek also published a smaller companion project called **deepseek-recipe**. That component handles token encoding and decoding, and its processing logic is aligned with the official DeepSeek API, meaning developers who self-host DeepInfer can expect the same tokenization behavior they would get calling DeepSeek’s hosted service. DeepSeek has said inference code for future models will continue to be added to the DeepInfer repository over time, suggesting this is the first entry in an ongoing release schedule rather than a one-off gesture. [SiliconANGLE’s coverage of the release](https://siliconangle.com/2026/10/20/deepseek-open-sources-deepinfer-the-inference-framework-behind-its-production-services/) frames DeepInfer specifically as “the inference framework behind its production services,” underlining that this is not a stripped-down demo but the same lineage of code DeepSeek uses to answer real customer traffic. That distinction, software built for a live production workload rather than a lab benchmark, is what separates this release from most open-source AI tooling. ## Inside DeepInfer: What the Framework Actually Does Documentation published with the release describes a set of capabilities aimed squarely at large-scale serving rather than single-GPU experimentation. LLMs.content: # Software Engineering 2026-10-20 | | Total: 42 ## [#1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26464 "1/42") [VerusEval: Evaluating LLM-Generated Verus Specifications Beyond Verifier Acceptance](/arxiv/2610.26464) [PDF] [Copy] [Kimi] [REL] **Authors**: [Ding Wang](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Ding Wang), [Chao Jiang](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Chao Jiang), [Dugang Liu](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Dugang Liu), [Zhiwu Xu](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Zhiwu Xu), [Cheng Wen](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Cheng Wen), [Zhong Ming](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Zhong Ming), [Yuwei Liu](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Yuwei Liu), [Xinyi Wan](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Xinyi Wan), [Lin Huang](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Lin Huang) Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate Verus contracts for Rust programs together with the proofs that establish them. Yet verifier acceptance, the common measure of success, shows only that the implementation satisfies the generated contract, so it leaves open whether the contract captures the intended behavior. Assessing specification generation therefore requires an evaluation methodology, not a single metric. We present VerusEval, a framework that evaluates generated contracts along six dimensions, including Verus-native checks for semantic triviality, validated input-output (I/O) suites, and contract equivalence, and that relates them so that the strength and blind spots of each become measurable. Evaluating 13,716 artifacts from four workflows, five LLMs, and two prompting settings on 762 tasks, we find that acceptance overstates quality: only 42.3\% of the accepted artifacts complete all three semantic checks without a flag, and across workflows and models, higher acceptance does not consistently come with more correct contracts. I/O evaluation rejects 23.6\% of the accepted artifacts, yet only 63.2\% of those that pass it are proved equivalent. Of the accepted artifacts flagged by contract comparison, 84.1\% have a rejected completeness obligation, and the direction of a failure prioritizes inspection of the generated contract or the reference; it does not by itself establish which artifact is defective. Screening and review further identify 36 candidate defects among 61 selected reference contracts, and repairing one of them makes 10 of its 11 failing artifacts equivalent. Based on these findings, we derive four actionable lessons for evaluation, generation, and benchmark maintenance. **Subject**: [Software Engineering](/arxiv/cs.SE) **Publish**: 2026-10-19 14:15:50 UTC --- ## [#2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26394 "2/42") [When Coding Agents Outpace Review: Evaluating PRD-Driven Development in Mature Enterprise Repositories](/arxiv/2610.26394) [PDF] [Copy] [Kimi] [REL] **Authors**: [Tianqi Liu](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Tianqi Liu), [Yandong Guan](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Yandong Guan), [Songze Li](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Songze Li), [Wenkai Wang](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Wenkai Wang), [Gang Yu](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Gang Yu), [Chengfei Lv](https://arxiv.org/search/?searchtype=author&query=Chengfei Lv) Coding agents increasingly undertake development tasks in mature enterprise repositories, yet existing benchmarks offer limited insight into whether they fulfill complete Product Requirement Documents (PRDs) and where delivery breaks down. AI Product.content: CFOtech Asia - Technology news for CFOs & financial decision-makers [![CFOtech Asia logo](/brands/cfo-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Bloomberg launches Enterprise MCP for AI data access](https://cfotech.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/20/tony-mcmanus-story-321815.webp) [Data governance](https://cfotech.asia/tag/data-governance) [Risk & Compliance](https://cfotech.asia/tag/risk-compliance) [GenAI](https://cfotech.asia/tag/generative-ai) # Bloomberg launches Enterprise MCP for AI data access Wed, 21st Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://cfotech.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Bloomberg has launched Enterprise MCP for its Data Licence Plus service, designed to connect Bloomberg data with clients' artificial intelligence applications. The system gives AI agents access to licensed Bloomberg data through a standardised interface covering more than 100 million securities and over 50,000 fields. The offering is intended to address a problem that has emerged as financial firms test generative AI tools: models may be able to reason over information, but often lack enough context to interpret market and reference data correctly. Enterprise MCP is an access layer over Data Licence Plus, Bloomberg's newer Data Licence product. It combines metadata on data fields with semantic search tools and workflow-specific functions, allowing users to request information in natural language instead of relying on field codes or manual identifier matching. The service can provide details including what a data field represents, how it was calculated, when it applies, and qualifiers such as currency, exchange, price type, period and date. It also includes entity resolution tools designed to map names, tickers or descriptions to the correct instrument and its links to the issuing company. Bloomberg is offering the product as an enterprise service in which it hosts and manages the access layer, while clients retain control over the AI agents and applications connected to it, including the models, prompts and instructions used in their workflows. That structure reflects a broader approach emerging in financial services, where firms want to use large language models and agent-based systems but remain cautious about data governance, entitlements and audit requirements. Under the new service, Bloomberg validates a firm's entitlements before returning data in response to an agent request under standard Data Licence rights. Requests are resolved against Bloomberg's Operational Datastore, while tool-level limits cap the number of securities and fields returned in a single call. **Workflow focus** The initial release includes what Bloomberg calls workflow skills, or reusable procedures tied to common financial tasks. These cover point-in-time universe retrieval, corporate action adjustment and revision history. The first set of skills will also help users identify outliers in a group of tickers, review trades that breach accepted price deviation thresholds, and assess securities and trades for possible sanctions exposure. Bloomberg is presenting the service as a way to reduce manual steps in research, portfolio management, risk and operations. In practice, that means reducing the work involved in locating the right dataset, matching identifiers and checking whether a figure is fit for a given task. Software stocks plunged earlier this year on concerns that AI-native applications from labs like Anthropic and OpenAI would disrupt entrenched software-as-a-service (SaaS) businesses with cheaper and more customizable programs. It makes devices like the Taser electrical weapon and body and dashboard cameras. That combination has given Axon a wide economic moat in serving law enforcement agencies, and it's reinforced that with a history of acquisitions and an innovative culture that has already rolled out a number of AI products. One of them is Draft One, a generative AI tool that writes first drafts of police reports based on camera footage. Over its history, Axon has been a top performer in the stock market, delivering consistently strong revenue growth as it expands its market opportunity. There isn't one specific issue that explains Axon's sell-off. Among the factors weighing on the stock are its valuation, concerns about margin compression, management's decision to cut cash flow guidance as it invests in the business, and a recent convertible debt offering. Currently, the stock trades at a [price-to-sales ratio](https://www.fool.com/terms/p/price-to-sales-ratio-value-stocks/) of 12, which is expensive but not excessively so. Around its peak last year, its P/S ratio was around 30, making it one of the most expensive software stocks on the market. The system applies security, policy and access controls to data wherever it is queried. Zetaris says this is intended to address a common obstacle in enterprise AI projects: models and agents can generate code quickly but still struggle to access current internal data safely. Vinay Samuel, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Zetaris, said the problem was slowing broader adoption of AI in business settings. "Coding harnesses have dramatically accelerated software development, but enterprise AI still struggles to access trustworthy, governed data," Samuel said. "Our AI Data Harness gives AI tools a real-time path to the data they need, wherever it lives, without forcing companies to centralize everything first." The event is framed as a test of whether AI coding tools can be paired with direct access to distributed enterprise data in live development settings. Developers will build enterprise AI applications using both systems together. "Putting these technologies in the hands of thousands of developers will show what becomes possible when AI agents can work with live enterprise data without sacrificing security," Samuel said. "The hackathon is designed to move that idea from theory into working applications." SpaceXAI described the pairing as a combination of coding tools and governed data access. "A coding harness is an important part of building enterprise AI applications. Also very important is instant access to relevant, governed data-the role of a data harness. Through the hackathon, developers will explore how Grok Build and Zetaris can be used together to combine these two complementary harnesses to build AI-enabled workflows. Organizations need a way to deliver responsive experiences for users, support agentic workloads, and maximize utilization of increasingly scarce compute resources. llm-d 1.0 is built to address these challenges through intelligent distributed inference capabilities to facilitate improvements in performance, increases in throughput and help organizations gain greater control over the economics of AI serving. **Turning Innovation into Production Reality** With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Open Source AI.content: 4 minute read # llm-d 1.0 hardens open-source AI inference for day 2 production operations The distributed inference framework makes serving large models on your own infrastructure reliable and affordable for the agentic era. Today at the PyTorch Conference North America, llm-d project contributors are announcing llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for open-source AI infrastructure. A Kubernetes-native [distributed inference serving network](https://research.ibm.com/blog/distributed-inference), llm-d makes it possible to deploy inference stacks for any model, on any accelerator, in any cloud. The release signals that llm-d has moved beyond demonstrating individual performance techniques and is ready to support the realities of production: sustained efficiency under many workloads, all while balancing service priorities amid growing demand. And with inference costs increasing, llm-d is meant to help bring model deployment in-house and deliver returns on AI investment. The work has been developed with a growing open-source community that includes hardware providers, model developers, cloud platforms, and enterprise users. As lead maintainers of llm-d, Red Hat, IBM, and Google have helped turn advanced inference techniques into a coordinated system that enterprises can operate at scale. The three co-founded llm-d last year with CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and industry leaders including AMD, Cisco, Hugging Face, Intel, Lambda, and Mistral AI have joined as contributors along the way. The result is a vendor-neutral alternative for organizations that want frontier-class inference performance without depending entirely on one proprietary model provider, cloud, or hardware platform. “llm-d is ready for day 2 operations,” said Carlos Costa, Distinguished Engineer at IBM Research, llm-d co-founder and lead maintainer. “llm-d has been delivering state-of-the-art inference performance for production workloads. What 1.0 adds is the maturity to run it like any other critical service: a stable API, multiple tenants with competing priorities sharing the same infrastructure, and upgrades that don't interrupt operations. That is what we built llm-d 1.0 to do.” ## A full production stack Since llm-d launched, the project has focused on five important approaches to improving AI inference: prefix-cache-aware routing, which directs a request to infrastructure that may already hold its shared context; KV-cache offloading, which expands the useful life of cached information by moving it across GPU, CPU, and storage resources; batch inference optimization, which groups work so infrastructure can process it more efficiently; prefill/decode disaggregation, which separates the work of reading a prompt from the work of generating a response; and wide expert parallelism, which distributes large mixture-of-experts models across many accelerators. These ideas are not new to version 1.0. What is new is the level of integration and operational maturity around them. With version 1.0, llm-d has matured into a stack capable of supporting day 2 operations: everything that must happen after an AI service is deployed. That includes serving workloads with competing priorities, managing different performance requirements, maintaining efficiency, prioritizing important services, and keeping the system dependable over time. A benchmark can show that one feature improves throughput, but a production system must keep delivering that performance when traffic changes, hardware fails, software is updated, or different users compete for the same resources. llm-d 1.0 is about making the individual techniques work together under those less predictable conditions. ## One endpoint, different kinds of work Expanding on the core technical innovations that have already made llm-d a powerful tool for distributed inference, llm-d 1.0 enhances support for multi-tenant quality of service, zero-downtime operations, and agent-aware serving, for sustained performance in common day 2 production operatio...

[Helical Insight](https://www.helicalinsight.com/), an open-source BI platform that get’s installed on-premises, now supports locally hosted language models, including those served through Ollama, so teams can adopt conversational analytics without handing data to an outside AI service. The problem: AI that sends data elsewhere Conversational BI works by passing a user’s question, schema details and sometimes result data to a language model. If that model is run by an external provider, the information travels beyond the company’s walls. For regulated sectors, that raises concerns about privacy, data residency and audit readiness. The solution: bring your own model Helical Insight’s AI analytics module lets customers choose and host their own model. Paired with an on-premises installation, the full path from question to answer can stay within the organization’s network. It turns PDFs and document images into Agent-Friendly data with SOTA accuracy and speed. **New York, NY · United States** (PRUnderground) October 20, 2026 The team behind SoMark today announced the open-source release of [OXR](https://github.com/SoMarkAI/OXR) (Optical Everything Recognition), a 1.3-billion-parameter document parsing model. It turns PDFs and document images into Agent-Friendly data in Markdown or JSON, with layout coordinates and reading order. The release combines what the team reports as state-of-the-art（SOTA） accuracy and parsing speed with a recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop used during post-training. According to [the evaluation report](https://github.com/BinyangQiu/OXR/blob/d33b33b3c80b9712e0ab529d06c68c69ee0f3a92/docs/benchmark.md), OXR ranks No. 1 on olmOCR-Bench, OmniDocBench, and DocParsingBench. The accuracy comparisons use published peer-model scores. In separate end-to-end speed tests on a single RTX PRO 6000, it ranked first among 21 compared models on the same 100-page OmniDocBench subset. OXR recognizes 13 document element types, including tables, formulas, chemical equations, chemical structures, and code blocks. Supported inputs include challenging documents and layouts, such as A3 exam papers, newspapers, vertical text, and handwritten content. It preserves document structure and reading order in its output, with layout coordinates linking parsed content to its position on the original page. This supports downstream retrieval and agent workflows. The model is intended for AI builders developing LLM applications, RAG systems, agents, and document workflows, as well as document AI researchers and open-source developers. > “Real documents keep exposing new weaknesses. Turning those failures into training data usually requires diagnosing the problems and manually labeling new samples,” said Binyang Qiu, founder and CEO of SoMark. “We wanted to speed up model iteration without waiting for another round of manual data preparation.” To address this evolving long-tail challenge, OXR incorporates an RSI loop into its post-training process, marking what the team describes as the first application of this approach in document parsing. The loop uses parsing errors and uncertain results to plan the next training round and generate targeted training data. In each round, OXR parses unlabeled documents. A general vision-language model (VLM) evaluates OXR outputs and analyzes errors and uncertainty, while disagreement across OXR rollouts also identifies uncertain samples. A clustering model groups these issues by cause. The general VLM then develops a training plan and generates targeted training data for OXR’s next training round. This loop requires no manual labeling of new training data, speeding up model iteration. While RSI supports continued model improvement, organizations also need parsing output that matches their own document standards. Even for the same document, businesses may define element categories, region boundaries, and grouping rules differently. OXR keeps layout analysis (LA) independent and pluggable, so teams can replace the built-in layout model while retaining OXR’s recognition and reading-order capabilities. OXR’s task-level architectural redesign also supports faster parsing. Recognition and reading order run in parallel within the same model, avoiding the delay of a separate reading-order step. Infra & Chips.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Intel’s 480GB AI Chip Takes Aim at Nvidia, AMD [2026] ![Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/droth.webp) [Daniel Roth](https://shattered.io/author/droth/) Updated Oct 20, 2026 · 14 min read Intel used the Open Compute Project Global Summit this month to put a name and a full spec sheet on the AI chip it had been teasing for more than a year. The Intel GPU D-series, built on the Xe3P architecture and previously known under the codename Crescent Island, packs up to 480GB of LPDDR5X memory onto a single air-cooled PCIe card. TechRadar framed the announcement under the headline “Inference is becoming the defining AI workload,” and that framing gets at what makes this launch worth paying attention to on October 20, 2026: Intel is not trying to out-FLOP Nvidia or AMD. It is trying to out-fit them, cramming more model into a single card so data centers need fewer cards to serve the same request. That distinction matters because the AI inference GPU market has quietly become the most contested piece of real estate in the data center. Training clusters get the headlines and the eye-watering price tags, but inference, the actual serving of chatbot replies, coding suggestions and agentic tasks to paying users, is where the volume lives and where the margins get squeezed. Intel’s bet is that memory capacity per card, not raw petaflops, is the lever that actually moves serving costs. Whether that bet pays off depends on factors Intel has not yet disclosed: price, availability, and independent benchmarks. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Intel Actually Announced at OCP 2026 The headline numbers, confirmed across multiple outlets covering the Open Compute Project Global Summit, are specific. The Intel GPU D-series delivers up to 480GB of LPDDR5X memory, 1.5TB/s of memory bandwidth, and 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute, all inside a 350-watt envelope that fits a standard, air-cooled PCIe card. That last detail is not a footnote. Most high-memory AI accelerators demand liquid cooling and custom rack infrastructure; Intel is explicitly positioning the D-series to drop into server chassis that already exist, according to coverage from [StorageReview](https://www.storagereview.com/news/intel-gpu-d-series-480gb-lpddr5x-1-3-pflops-fp8-350w-pcie-card). There is a wrinkle in the headline figure worth flagging before anyone builds a budget around it. The 480GB ceiling applies only to partner-built cards from ODMs and server vendors. Intel’s own branded card carries 160GB, a meaningful gap that [XenoSpectrum’s breakdown of the D-series memory tiers](https://xenospectrum.com/en/intel-d-series-inference-memory-bandwidth/) lays out in detail. Intel’s product page for the [GPU D270, its inference-optimized data center card](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/products/details/discrete-gpus/data-center-gpu/d-series.html), confirms the 480GB LPDDR5X figure as the top-end configuration rather than a universal spec across every SKU. Intel says a single D-series card can host models of up to roughly 300 billion parameters, and that an eight-GPU system can support more than one trillion parameters in aggregate. Those are Intel’s own claims, disclosed at the summit rather than validated by a third-party benchmark. We covered the full spec reveal in detail in our [report on the Crescent Island GPU D-series launch](https://shattered.io/intel-crescent-island-gpu-d-series-1-3-pflops-2026/); this piece picks up where that one left off, focused on what the launch means competitively rather than just what the card contains. ## Intel GPU D-series: The Full Spec Sheet | Specification | Intel GPU D-series | | --- | --- | | Codename | Crescent ...

[2] Oct 20, 2026 ![](/image/iso_banner.png) **SAN JOSE, C.A., OCT. 20, 2026** – Today, llm-d project contributors announced the release of llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for the open source project designed to help organizations deploy and scale large language model inference more efficiently across modern infrastructure. Founded [in 2025](https://llm-d.ai/blog/llm-d-press-release) by Red Hat, IBM (NYSE: [IBM](http://www.ibm.com/investor)), Google Cloud, CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), llm-d plays a key role in the open foundation for enterprises deploying AI at scale in production. As organizations race to put AI into production, many are discovering that running AI at scale can be as challenging and expensive as building the models themselves. Organizations need a way to deliver responsive experiences for users, support agentic workloads, and maximize utilization of increasingly scarce compute resources. llm-d 1.0 is built to address these challenges through intelligent distributed inference capabilities to facilitate improvements in performance, increases in throughput and help organizations gain greater control over the economics of AI serving. **Turning Innovation into Production Reality** With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Agentic workloads continually access and reuse vast amounts of context while supporting parallel agents that can generate unpredictable bursts of activity. Managing that context often consumes more resources than generating the final output itself, making latency, throughput, memory efficiency and infrastructure costs critical factors in realizing AI ROI. llm-d already delivers hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box for complex infrastructure environments, as well as prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch and async inference — across multiple model servers, including vLLM and SGLang. llm-d 1.0 is engineered to bring that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations and the ongoing work of running inference in production: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, providing with zero downtime features and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into a platform. New capabilities in 1.0 include: * **Multi-tenant quality of service** — Priority and fairness-aware flow control helps latency-sensitive requests, and bursty agent workloads share a fleet without starving one another. * **Zero-downtime operations** — Router high availability with hot standby and rolling updates keep traffic flowing through upgrades and planned maintenance. As organizations race to put AI into production, many are discovering that running AI at scale can be as challenging and expensive as building the models themselves. Organizations need a way to deliver responsive experiences for users, support agentic workloads, and maximize utilization of increasingly scarce compute resources. llm-d 1.0 is built to address these challenges through intelligent distributed inference capabilities to facilitate improvements in performance, increases in throughput and help organizations gain greater control over the economics of AI serving. **Turning Innovation into Production Reality** With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Agentic workloads continually access and reuse vast amounts of context while supporting parallel agents that can generate unpredictable bursts of activity. Managing that context often consumes more resources than generating the final output itself, making latency, throughput, memory efficiency and infrastructure costs critical factors in realizing AI ROI. llm-d already delivers hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box for complex infrastructure environments, as well as prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch and async inference — across multiple model servers, including vLLM and SGLang. llm-d 1.0 is engineered to bring that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations and the ongoing work of running inference in production: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, providing with zero downtime features and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into a platform. Today, the project includes more than 500 contributors from over 25 organizations collaborating on the future of distributed AI serving and helping build common foundations across the AI infrastructure stack. Infra & Chips.content: DataCenterNews US - Specialist news for cloud & data center decision-makers [![DataCenterNews US logo](/brands/dcn-new-logo.svg) United States](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.com) ![Five Nines Global & Nexus Core plan Casablanca AI centre](https://datacenter.news/uploads/story/2026/10/21/Stage_2_-_Architectural_plan_developed_by_the_consultants-3-story-321897.webp) [DC](https://datacenter.news/tag/data-centers) [HPC](https://datacenter.news/tag/high-performance-computing) [AI](https://datacenter.news/tag/artificial-intelligence) # Five Nines Global & Nexus Core plan Casablanca AI centre Tue, 20th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Sofiah Nichole Salivio](https://datacenter.news/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNywicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--3f3cbcdb3f86206827b894ccc07566b24a1d49e6/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/unnamed%20(2).webp) SOFIAH NICHOLE SALIVIO News Editor](/author/sofiah-nichole-salivio) Five Nines Global has partnered with Nexus Core Systems to develop a 20MW AI data centre near Casablanca as part of the wider 180MW Nexus AI Factory scheme. Both companies are registered in the UK. The planned facility is designed around Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 architecture and is described as renewable-powered. The deal brings together a UK-registered engineering and project partner and a UK-registered systems business on an African data infrastructure project aimed at AI workloads. It also puts Nvidia's latest server architecture at the centre of the first announced phase. The 20MW site is planned near Casablanca, Morocco, and forms part of the larger Nexus AI Factory programme, which has a total planned size of 180MW. **Project scope** The initial 20MW facility is a substantial build in its own right, even before the wider campus is considered. Set within a 180MW scheme, it points to a multi-stage approach to AI-focused data centre construction in North Africa. The use of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 architecture suggests the site is intended for intensive AI computing rather than conventional enterprise hosting alone. Large AI data centres are increasingly designed around tightly integrated compute clusters, dense power delivery and specialist cooling systems, making design and delivery more complex than for standard colocation developments. Renewable energy is another notable feature of the outline released by the companies. Power sourcing has become a central issue for AI data centre developers as model training and inference workloads increase electricity demand and intensify scrutiny of grid access, cost and emissions. **Regional angle** For UK readers, the relevance lies in the role of two UK-registered companies in a major overseas infrastructure project. British technology, engineering and advisory firms have increasingly looked to international data centre markets as demand for AI infrastructure outpaces available supply in established hubs. Morocco has attracted growing attention as a location for digital infrastructure because of its position between European, African and Middle Eastern markets, as well as its renewable energy ambitions. Developers have also examined the country's potential to match power availability with rising demand for regional cloud and AI services. The project near Casablanca reflects a broader pattern in which AI infrastructure investment is no longer confined to traditional data centre centres in Western Europe and North America. Developers are instead assessing sites where land, energy strategy and regional connectivity may support large-scale computing estates. **Technology focus** Nvidia's newest AI systems have become a key reference point for developers pitching large compute sites to customers and investors. Infra & Chips.content: # AI chip stocks bounce back as hyperscaler earnings loom, META equity raise in focus NVIDIA collects a check whether hyperscalers borrow, issue stock, or drain their cash reserves, but Meta faces a funding squeeze that could reshape what shareholders actually own. The size of one expected equity offering may decide how this AI spending… ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/dac1a1f2adf30aac00a449ddbb2a0950?s=44&d=mm&r=g) ## Quick Read ![A digital graphic set against a blue background shows various financial charts, including bar graphs and line graphs, with an overall upward trend. A large white arrow points diagonally upwards from the bottom left to the top right. Superimposed across the middle is a stylized optical fiber cable, depicted as a bundle of glowing blue and teal strands, suggesting high-speed data transmission. The image conveys themes of technological advancement and market growth.](https://247wallst.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/shutterstock_2630545873-400x213.jpg) Chip stocks bounced on October 19, and the session showed who collects the money in this AI cycle. The Nasdaq rose 1.3% with semiconductors leading; **NVIDIA** ([NASDAQ:NVDA](https://247wallst.com/companies/NVDA/) | [NVDA Price Prediction](https://247wallst.com/companies/nvda/price-prediction)) gained 1.38%, and **Meta Platforms** ([NASDAQ:META](https://247wallst.com/companies/META/)) slipped 0.55%. Seema Mody’s segment that day focused on that split. The GPU supplier rose while the hyperscaler expected to raise outside money fell behind, although one session cannot show that equity talk drove Meta lower. Meta’s expansion now needs more than its own cash. It guided 2026 capital expenditures to $130 billion to $145 billion, and [second-quarter free cash flow](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1326801/000162828026050596/meta-06302026xexhibit991.htm) fell to $784 million from $8.55 billion a year earlier. NVIDIA reported $96.22 billion in quarterly revenue, up 105.8%. That gap between the buyer’s falling cash and the seller’s rising sales is why the coming hyperscaler reports carry more weight than a typical quarter. ## Why This Pullback Could Precede Strong Hyperscaler Reports Mody cited Evercore ISI: “Evercore ISI out with a note this morning that leans a bit more bullish saying the pullback that we’ve recently seen in these names comes ahead of what they think will be a strong hyperscaler earnings season.” The firm reads recent weakness as a setup for those reports. NVIDIA is still down 4.08% over the past week and 2.33% over the past month, although it is up 16.67% year to date. Meta fell 5.05% over the past week and is down 1.28% over the past year despite a 7.13% gain in 2026. The weak one-year return suggests some investors likely doubt the payoff from the spending. Watch capital spending plans, AI revenue, and how the spending gets financed. NVIDIA expects top five hyperscaler capex to reach nearly $800 billion in 2026. ## Older NVIDIA Chips Still Hold Their Value Mody noted: “The H100 that’s Nvidia’s older chip has held up in terms of pricing ever since Anthropic’s latest model came out.” New model launches are lifting demand for older hardware too. That signals demand for compute still exceeds supply. NVIDIA said it has supply for about 70% of demand. It also protects collateral, because GPUs now back loans. Chips that hold their rental rates also hold their value as loan collateral. Asia is more cautious: “Bank of America’s semiconductor team just returning from Asia, sharing with clients that investors there are a bit more anxious about the AI funding cycle.” The worry there centers on funding. ## GPU-Backed Loans Are Becoming the Default Mody said: “Consensus amongst credit folks we spoke to over the weekend is that GPU backed loans will be the go to option for these companies.
